titles.636: Annotatio V §.III open: Lutherans admit double food/eating — yet extend corporal beyond its sphere
titles.637: Annotatio V §.III: invent double corporal eating; restrict Christ’s-body eating to mouth alone — call it Oral
titles.638: Annotatio V §.III: still Capernaite; Oral preached supernatural/sacramental — three Eucharistic species
titles.639: Annotatio V §.III: Selneccer — natural of elements; supernatural of body; spiritual of fruit — triple
titles.640: Annotatio V §.III close: Neoterici make Oral fundamental; Tertullian twist; Mayer on Spener — stop before §.IV

latin.636: §. III. Etsi verò Lutherus & quotquot à Luthero denominari gestiunt, cum, duplicem duntaxat in S. Cœna cibum, tùm, ob duplicem hunc cibum, duplicem expositam Manducationem, corporalem panis, & spiritualem Corporis Christi, nulli diffitentur; tamen Corporalem extra objecti sui adæquati, corporalis scil. cibi sphæram, inde extensuri, quod præter corporalem manducationem, veram nullam dari posse, nimis crasse concipiunt, duplicem Corporalem comminiscuntur Manducationem, panis unam, alteram Corporis Christi.
latin.637: quarum posterior, ut minùs appareat Capernaitica (1) ad solum os corporis restringunt, Januam dentium, gutturis deglutitionem & in stomachum intromissionem hinc procul abesse jubentes, eóque Corporalem Corporis Christi Manducationem suam, à solius oris corporalis denominatione, Oralem salutantes.
latin.638: (2) Dùm adhuc sic Capernaiticæ Manducationis, saltem partialis, species non omnis abolita, imò verò satis clarè pellucet, Oralem Corporis Christi Manducationem suam, Supernaturalem prædicant & Sacramentalem, hôc pactò in universum tres in Cœna sacra Manducandi modos, seu Manducationis Eucharisticæ tres Species, inculcantes. Corporalem panis meréque Physicam; Corporalem seu Oralem Corporis Christi, quæ etiam sit supernaturalis & sacramentalis; denique Spiritualem non tàm corporis Christi, quam fructuum & efficaciæ hujus.
latin.639: Sic enim quærit Nicol. Selneccerus, in libello brevi de Cœna Domini: Quotuplex est manducatio, ait, in S. Cœna? & respondet: Cum Christus panem sumat, frangat porrigat discipulis, & Paulus dicat: Quotiescunque manducabitis panem hunc &c. manifestum est, Manducationem naturalem & physicam ponendam esse, non corporis aut sanguinis Christi, sed elementorum, panis & vini. Hæc enim elementa non transsubstantiantur in corpus & sanguinem Christi, sed naturam suam retinent, digeruntur, & coquuntur, & absumuntur. Cùm verò non tantum panis manducetur in Cœna, Sed Christus de pane dicat: Accipite, edite, hoc est Corpus meum, ideo manducatio supernaturalis & cælestis ponenda est, quæ est invisibilis & insensibilis, & tamen veri & Substantialís corporis Christi manducatio juxta verba institutionis Christi. Et quia promissio addita est verbis Institutionis, quia beneficiorum Christi applicatio fit per fidem, ad vitam & salutem æternam, ideò & Spiritualis manducatio locum necessariò habet, & ita triplex Manducatio piè & verè poni potest: Manducatio Naturalis, seu physica, quæ ad elementa visibilia & sensibilia, panem & vinum pertinet: Manducatio Sacramentalis, quæ ad verum corpus & sanguinem Christi, quod cum pane exhibetur & accipitur, & qui cum vino datur & bibitur, referenda est: Et Manducatio Spiritualis, quæ tantum est de fructu, & efficacia salutaris sumtionis intelligenda.
latin.640: Quin Neoterici Lutheranorum plurimi, hosque inter Wittebergensis quidam, non pro veritate duntaxat Trigæ manducationis, sed & pro necessitate ejusdem ad salutem, certè pro Fundamentalitate Oralis Corporis Christi Manducationis, in relatione ad fidem Christianam, graviter depugnant, fundamentaliter à se pariter atque à fide Christiana dissidere, clamitando, quotquot Oralem Corporis Christi Manducationem, Supernaturali licèt Spiritualique enixissimè adstructa, inficiantur, utut in Scriptura & primitiva Ecclesia prorsus inauditam, & nonnisi ex unius Tertulliani dictione hac, partim obscura, partim æquivoca, partim denique Rhetorica: (Caro, Corpore & sanguine Christi vescitur, ut & anima de Deo saginetur. Libro de Resurrectione) Bajerianis fidiculis Compend. Theolog. Historic. p. 586. initio, extortum, de quo tamen Tertulliano quid sentiendum, quóve locô hujus Auctoritas habenda sit, vel novissimè Celeberrimi nominis honorisque Theologus Joh. Frid. Mayerus, haud obscurè subinnuit, quando piæ memoriæ Philipp. Jacob. Spenerum, Lutheranæ Ecclesiæ parti maximæ mirè exosum, nostræ ætatis Tertullianum jure dicendum arbitratur, Bibliothec. Scriptor. Theologiæ Moralis, pag. 27.

pass_a.636: §. III. Although indeed Luther and whoever desire to be named from Luther deny to no one both a merely double food in the Sacred Supper and, on account of this double food, a double Eating set forth — corporal of the bread, and spiritual of Christ’s Body — yet, about to extend the Corporal beyond the sphere of its adequate object, namely corporal food, from this, that they conceive too grossly that besides corporal eating no true eating can be given, they invent a double Corporal Eating — one of bread, the other of Christ’s Body.
pass_a.637: Of which the latter, that it may appear less Capernaite, (1) they restrict to the body’s mouth alone, ordering the gate of the teeth, the throat’s swallowing, and introduction into the stomach to be far away from here — and so greeting their Corporal Eating of Christ’s Body, from the denomination of the corporal mouth alone, as Oral.
pass_a.638: (2) While still thus not every appearance of Capernaite Eating — at least partial — is abolished, nay rather shines clearly enough, they preach their Oral Eating of Christ’s Body as Supernatural and Sacramental, and by this pact inculcate in the Sacred Supper altogether three modes of Eating, or three Species of Eucharistic Eating: the Corporal of bread and merely Physical; the Corporal or Oral of Christ’s Body, which is also supernatural and sacramental; and finally the Spiritual not so much of Christ’s body as of its fruits and efficacy.
pass_a.639: For so Nicol. Selneccerus asks in a short booklet on the Lord’s Supper: How manifold is eating, he says, in the Sacred Supper? and answers: Since Christ takes bread, breaks it, hands it to the disciples, and Paul says: As often as you shall eat this bread &c., it is manifest that a natural and physical Eating is to be posited — not of Christ’s body or blood, but of the elements, bread and wine. For these elements are not transubstantiated into Christ’s body and blood, but retain their nature, are digested, cooked, and consumed. But since not only bread is eaten in the Supper, but Christ says of the bread: Take, eat, this is my Body, therefore a supernatural and heavenly eating is to be posited, which is invisible and insensible, and yet an eating of Christ’s true and Substantial body according to Christ’s Institution words. And because a promise is added to the Institution words, because the application of Christ’s benefits is made by faith unto eternal life and salvation, therefore Spiritual eating also necessarily has place, and so a triple Eating can piously and truly be posited: Natural or physical Eating, which pertains to the visible and sensible elements, bread and wine; Sacramental Eating, which is to be referred to Christ’s true body and blood, which with the bread is exhibited and received, and which with the wine is given and drunk; And Spiritual Eating, which is to be understood only of the fruit and efficacy of salutary reception.
pass_a.640: Nay most of the Lutherans’ Neoterics — and among them a certain Wittenberger — fight gravely not only for the truth of the Triple of eating, but also for its necessity to salvation, certainly for the Fundamentality of the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body in relation to the Christian faith, crying that whoever deny the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body — even with the Supernatural and Spiritual most earnestly built up — dissent fundamentally alike from them and from the Christian faith, although it is altogether unheard in Scripture and the primitive Church, and extorted only from one saying of Tertullian, partly obscure, partly equivocal, partly finally Rhetorical — (Flesh is fed with Christ’s Body and blood, that the soul also may be fattened from God. Book on the Resurrection) — by Bajer’s little strings, Compend. Theolog. Historic. p. 586 beginning; concerning which Tertullian yet what is to be thought, and in what place his Authority is to be held, even most lately the Theologian of most celebrated name and honor Joh. Frid. Mayer not obscurely hints, when he judges Philipp. Jacob. Spener of pious memory — wondrously hated by the greatest part of the Lutheran Church — rightly to be called the Tertullian of our age, Bibliothec. Scriptor. Theologiæ Moralis, p. 27.

636: §.III: Luther and his namesakes grant a double Supper-food and a double eating — corporal of bread, spiritual of Christ’s Body.

Yet because they grossly hold that nothing but corporal eating is true, they stretch the corporal beyond corporal food’s proper sphere and invent a double corporal eating: one of bread, one of Christ’s Body.
637: To look less Capernaite they restrict the second corporal eating to the mouth alone — teeth’s gate, throat-swallow, and stomach entry ordered far off.
From the mouth’s name alone they salute that corporal eating of Christ’s Body as Oral.
638: Even so a Capernaite look (at least partial) still shows clearly. They then preach that Oral eating as Supernatural and Sacramental.
Result: three Eucharistic species — merely physical of bread; corporal/oral of Christ’s Body (also supernatural/sacramental); spiritual not so much of the body as of its fruits and efficacy.
639: Selneccer’s short booklet on the Lord’s Supper asks how manifold eating is and answers with a triple: natural/physical of the elements (bread and wine keep their nature, are digested); supernatural/heavenly of Christ’s true substantial body (invisible, per Institution); spiritual of the fruit and efficacy of salutary reception by faith.
So: Natural, Sacramental, and Spiritual — piously and truly posited.
640: §.III close: many Lutheran Neoterics (a Wittenberger among them) fight not only for the triple’s truth but for Oral’s necessity and fundamentality to Christian faith — branding deniers of Oral (even with spiritual stressed) as fundamental dissenters.

The Oral claim is unheard in Scripture and the primitive Church, and is twisted from one partly rhetorical Tertullian line (Bajer, Compend. p. 586); Mayer hints Spener is rightly called our age’s Tertullian (Bibl. Theol. Mor. p. 27). Stop before §.IV.
